items.title: A base bigger than the number
items.prose: Think of 8 as a power of 2, or use the change of base rule.
items.question: What is $\log_8 2$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which power of 8 is its cube root?

byKey.swap: You found $\log_2 8$. Here 8 is the base, and 2 is smaller than 8.
byKey.div: You divided 8 by 2. The log is a power on 8.

explain.text: $8 = 2^3$, so $2 = 8^{1/3}$ and $\log_8 2 = \tfrac{1}{3}$. By the change of base rule, $\tfrac{\log 2}{\log 8} = \tfrac{0.301}{0.903} = \tfrac{1}{3}$ too.

items.title: Roots inside a log
items.prose: Let $p = \log_b x$ and $q = \log_b y$, with $x$ and $y$ positive.
items.question: Write $\log_b \dfrac{x^3}{\sqrt{y}}$ in terms of $p$ and $q$.

widget.label: log of x cubed over root y

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\sqrt{y}$ as $y^{1/2}$, then use the quotient and power laws.

byKey.root-inside: You took the root of the log. $\sqrt{y} = y^{1/2}$, so the power law gives $\tfrac{1}{2}q$.
byKey.divide: You divided the logs. A quotient inside the log becomes a difference.
byKey.no-half: You dropped the square root. $\sqrt{y}$ is $y^{1/2}$, so its log is $\tfrac{1}{2}q$.

explain.text: $\sqrt{y} = y^{1/2}$. The quotient law gives $\log_b x^3 - \log_b y^{1/2}$, and the power law gives $3p - \tfrac{1}{2}q$.

items.title: Equal falls on a log chart
items.prose: On a log-price chart, share A falls from £80.00 to £60.00. Share B, at £24.00, falls by the same height on the chart.
items.question: What is share B's new price?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Equal heights on a log chart are equal ratios.

byKey.pounds: You took away the same £20.00. From £24.00 that would be a fall of 83%, not 25%.
byKey.same-end: Equal heights do not mean equal end prices. Copy the ratio: ×0.75.

explain.text: A's fall is £60.00 ÷ £80.00 = 0.75, a height of $\log 0.75 \approx -0.125$. The same height from £24.00 gives £24.00 × 0.75 = £18.00. Both shares lost 25%.

items.title: A long losing streak
items.prose: A strategy loses 15% of its capital in each losing month. It starts with £12,000.00 and has nothing but losing months.
items.question: After how many months is the capital first below £3,000.00?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $0.85^n = 0.25$, then round up.

byKey.simple: You took £1,800.00 off each month. Each loss is 15% of what is left, so the losses shrink.
byKey.short: After 8 months the capital is £3,269.89, still above £3,000.00.
byKey.raw: That is the exact solution, 8.53. Months come whole, so the first month below is the next one.

explain.text: We need $0.85^n < \tfrac{3000}{12000} = 0.25$. Logs give $n > \tfrac{\log 0.25}{\log 0.85} = \tfrac{-0.6021}{-0.0706} \approx 8.53$, so 9 months. Dividing by a negative log flips the inequality, which is why we get $>$.

items.title: Many forms of one log
items.question: Which of these equal $\log_2 50$? Select all that apply.

options.why: That is $\log \tfrac{50}{2}$, about 1.398. A quotient of logs is not the log of a quotient.
That divides the numbers, giving 25. The rule divides their logs.

feedback.correct: Any base works for the change of base rule, and the laws split 50 as $2 \times 5^2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each option on a calculator, or rewrite 50 as $2 \times 25$.

explain.text: The change of base rule works with any base on top and bottom, so both quotients are right. $50 = 2 \times 25 = 2 \times 5^2$, so $\log_2 50 = 1 + \log_2 25 = 1 + 2\log_2 5$. The other two give 1.398 and 25.

items.title: Proving the power law
items.prose: Prove the power law $\log_b(x^k) = k \log_b x$ from the index law $(b^m)^k = b^{mk}$.
items.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: By the meaning of a log, $x = b^m$.
Raise both sides to the power $k$: $x^k = (b^m)^k = b^{mk}$, by the index law.
By the meaning of a log again, $\log_b(x^k) = mk$.

feedback.correct: Name, rewrite as a power, use the index law, read the log, substitute.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need $x$ as a power of $b$ before you can raise it to $k$.

explain.text: Writing $x = b^m$ lets the index law act on $x^k$. Reading $b^{mk}$ as a log gives $mk$, which is $k \log_b x$.

items.title: The slower start that wins
items.prose: Position A is worth £400.00 and grows 9% a year. Position B is worth £1,000.00 and grows 3% a year. Both compound yearly.
items.question: After how many whole years is A first worth more than B?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $400 \times 1.09^n > 1000 \times 1.03^n$ and collect the powers on one side.

byKey.short: After 16 years A is worth £1,588.12 and B £1,604.71. A is still behind.
byKey.raw: That is the exact crossing, 16.18. The first whole year after it is 17.

explain.text: Divide by $400 \times 1.03^n$: $\left(\tfrac{1.09}{1.03}\right)^n > 2.5$. Logs give $n > \tfrac{\log 2.5}{\log 1.0583} \approx 16.18$. At 17 years A is worth £1,731.05 and B £1,652.85.

items.title: Doubling time, derived and tested
items.prompt: A deposit of £$P$ grows at a rate $r$ a year, compounded yearly. (a) Show that the time to double is $n = \dfrac{\log 2}{\log(1 + r)}$, justifying each step. (b) Find the first whole year in which £1,000.00 at 7% is worth more than £2,000.00. Give its balance then. (c) A colleague says that at 14% the money doubles in exactly half the time it takes at 7%. Test the claim, and explain what you find.
items.model:
**(a)** Doubling means $P(1 + r)^n = 2P$.

Divide both sides by $P$, which is positive: $(1 + r)^n = 2$. The deposit cancels, so the answer does not depend on $P$.

Take $\log$ of both sides: $\log\big((1 + r)^n\big) = \log 2$.

By the power law, $n \log(1 + r) = \log 2$.

Since $r > 0$, $1 + r > 1$ and $\log(1 + r) > 0$, so we may divide: $n = \dfrac{\log 2}{\log(1 + r)}$.

**(b)** With $r = 0.07$: $n = \dfrac{0.30103}{0.02938} \approx 10.24$ years. After 10 years the balance is $1000 \times 1.07^{10} = \text{£}1{,}967.15$, still short. After 11 years it is $1000 \times 1.07^{11} = \text{£}2{,}104.85$. So year 11 is the first year above £2,000.00.

**(c)** With $r = 0.14$: $n = \dfrac{0.30103}{0.05690} \approx 5.29$ years. Half of 10.24 is 5.12, so the claim is close but false. The reason is that $\log(1.14)$ is not $2\log(1.07)$: by the power law $2\log 1.07 = \log(1.07^2) = \log 1.1449$, and $1.14 < 1.1449$. Doubling the rate does not square the growth factor, so the doubling time falls by a little less than half.

rubric.text: Sets up $P(1 + r)^n = 2P$ and cancels $P$, noting the answer does not depend on $P$.
Takes logs of both sides and uses the power law, naming it.
Divides by $\log(1 + r)$ and says why it is not zero (it is positive).
Finds $n \approx 10.24$ and concludes the first whole year is 11, checking year 10 falls short.
Finds about 5.29 years at 14%, compares with 5.12, and explains that $\log 1.14 \neq 2 \log 1.07$ because $1.07^2 = 1.1449$.
